Question: Two real numbers are selected independently at random from the interval \([-20, 10].\) What is the probability that the product of those numbers is greater than zero?
Solution:
Method 1: Add the two same-sign probabilities

Use the standard interpretation that each draw is uniform on \([-20,10]\). A product is positive exactly when both numbers are negative or both are positive.

The whole interval has length \(30\). Its negative portion has length \(20\), and its positive portion has length \(10\), so a single draw is negative with probability \(2/3\) and positive with probability \(1/3\). Drawing exactly zero has probability zero because a single point has length zero.

Independence lets us multiply the probabilities for the two draws. The two favorable cases cannot occur together, so their probabilities add:
\[
P(\text{positive product})
=\left(\frac23\right)^2+\left(\frac13\right)^2
=\frac49+\frac19
=\boxed{\frac59}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

Method 2: Compare favorable areas

Interpret both selections as uniform on \([-20,10]\). Represent the selected numbers by an ordered pair \((u,v)\). Because the selections are independent, the pair is uniform in the square
\[
[-20,10]\times[-20,10],
\]
whose area is \(30^2=900\).

The condition \(uv>0\) describes two disjoint regions. Both coordinates can be negative, giving a square of side \(20\), or both can be positive, giving a square of side \(10\). These have total area
\[
20^2+10^2=500.
\]
The coordinate axes are excluded because they give product zero; excluding these line segments does not change area. Thus
\[
P(uv>0)=\frac{500}{900}=\boxed{\frac59},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
